slides.title: How CSRF works
slides.summary: Another site makes the user's browser send a request to yours, and the browser attaches the user's cookies.
body: Browsers attach cookies to requests based on where they're going, not where they came from. A malicious page can submit a form to your site, and the logged-in user's session cookie goes with it.
The attacker can't read the response (the same-origin policy stops that), but they don't need to: the damage is the action itself.
<mark>Any state-changing request authenticated only by cookies is a CSRF target.</mark>

body.note: Using GET for actions (/delete?id=5) makes it worse: a simple <img> tag is enough to trigger it.

steps.caption: A normal session in another tab.
The page contains a hidden form.
The browser sends the user's cookie along.
Nothing in the request tells the bank it was forged.

slides.title: Defending against CSRF
slides.summary: SameSite cookies are the baseline; add tokens or origin checks for anything sensitive.

ul: SameSite cookies: Lax stops cookies on cross-site POSTs and subresource requests; Strict also drops them on cross-site links. Set it explicitly rather than relying on browser defaults.
CSRF tokens: a random value tied to the session, sent in a header or hidden field. A cross-site page can't read it, so it can't include it.
Check Origin / Sec-Fetch-Site: reject state-changing requests from other sites.

body: <mark>Combine SameSite cookies with tokens or origin checks: each covers gaps in the other.</mark>

body.text: Angular's HttpClient reads an XSRF-TOKEN cookie and sends it back as an X-XSRF-TOKEN header on mutating requests to the same origin (the double-submit pattern). The server sets the cookie and checks they match.
